answer: The provided passages do not specify any additional international or domestic lists beyond the UNSC Sanctions Lists, the lists in the Schedules to the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism (Implementation of Security Council Resolutions) Order, 2007, and the UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List of Designated Individuals and Entities.

The bank shall ensure adherence to the provisions of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and the Rules made thereunder [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications issued from time to time by the RBI based on advice received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India [S1].
A commercial bank must review its money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment at least annually [S1].

The bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e-documents thereof or Form No. 60 [S1]. Before doing so, the bank must give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard [S1].

The commercial bank must monitor the 'at par' cheque facility and review such arrangements to assess risks, including credit and reputational risk [S4]. Additionally, the bank must retain the right to verify the records maintained by the customer co-operative banks for compliance with KYC and AML instructions [S4].
For a remittance of ₹50,000 or more, a commercial bank must effect the transaction by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques, and not against cash payment [S1].

A commercial bank should consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time, as well as publicly available information, to identify countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations [S1].
Under the general restriction, a commercial bank shall not collect account payee cheques for any person other than the payee constituent [S1].

The bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government [S2].
The disclosures required by the RBI are intended only to supplement and not to replace disclosure requirements under other laws, regulations, or accounting and financial reporting standards [S3].
Yes, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP to carry out CDD for new customer onboarding, which includes individual customers and Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers [S1].

Under the RBI's KYC Directions for commercial banks, if there is no change in the KYC information of a Legal Entity customer, the bank must obtain a self-declaration through registered email, digital channels, or official letters, and ensure that Beneficial Ownership information is accurate and updated [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure it holds KYC documents compliant with current CDD standards and verify the customer’s PAN details from the issuing authority's database during periodic updation [S1].

Under the RBI KYC Directions, a commercial bank must obtain any two of the listed documents or their equivalent e-documents as proof of business for a sole proprietary firm [S1]. However, if the bank is satisfied that it is not possible to furnish two such documents, it may accept only one document at its discretion, provided it undertakes contact point verification and confirms the business activity from the address [S3].
No, the bank shall not require CDD of all the members of an SHG while opening the savings bank account [S1]. The CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].
Under the RBI KYC Directions, a commercial bank must categorize its customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on its assessment and risk perception [S1].

Under the RBI's KYC Directions, a commercial bank must review the risk categorisation of accounts at least once every six months [S1]. Additionally, the bank must perform periodic updation of KYC at least once every two years for high-risk customers, once every eight years for medium-risk customers, and once every ten years for low-risk customers [S4].

Under the financial education provision, a bank shall disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to the customers so that the customers can make an informed judgment about their choice of products [S1].

The bank must lay down a transparent, non-discretionary, and non-discriminatory policy for the renewal of overdue term deposits, notifying the customer of the terms and conditions, including interest rates, at the time of acceptance [S1]. Additionally, if there is no explicit mandate to renew, the bank must conduct an annual review of such accounts to prevent them from becoming unclaimed and inform the depositors in writing [S4].
Yes, the Directions repeal existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Responsible Business Conduct as applicable to Commercial Banks [S4].

The bank must make all printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, available in trilingual form, which is English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language [S1].

A commercial bank must ensure that necessary infrastructure and facilities are put in place and appropriate security measures are taken in each of its branches where loans are sanctioned against gold and/or silver collateral [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure that the gold and/or silver collateral is handled only in its branches and only by its employees [S1].

A commercial bank shall be guided by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S1]. These Directions are formally titled the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S3].

For claims related to safe deposit lockers or articles in safe custody, the bank must pay compensation at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay if it does not adhere to the prescribed timeline [S1].
To facilitate interaction between the bank and exporters, the bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with a concentration of exporters [S1].

The policy must cover the auction procedure, including the trigger event for the auction and the timeline for serving an auction notice, as well as the mode of auction and the empanelment of auctioneers [S1]. Additionally, it must specify the notice period allowed to the borrower or legal heirs for settling the loan before the auction takes place [S1].

Yes, a bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum in a BSBD account, with or without charges, provided it is done in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure [S1]. However, the bank shall not require the customer to maintain a minimum balance in the account to avail of these additional facilities [S1].
The bank shall undertake at least an annual review in respect of accounts where there is no customer-induced transaction for more than a year [S1].
Such messages may be displayed or distributed in bank branches, as well as at places like ATMs or Business Correspondent Points, to ensure wider visibility and easy notice by customers [S1].

Yes, a commercial bank is held responsible for the actions of its agents, as it is considered the principal in this relationship [S2]. Consequently, the bank must ensure that its recovery agents strictly adhere to the prescribed instructions while engaged in the recovery of dues [S2].
The “Enquiry” or “May I Help You” counter should be located near the entry point of the banking hall [S1]. This requirement applies to all branches, excluding very small branches [S1].
The prescribed post-shipment interest rate ceases from the date the foreign currency amounts are credited to the banks' 'Nostro' accounts [S1].
The bank shall undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees, or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts or unclaimed deposits [S1].

A commercial bank must conduct regular audits of its service providers, including subcontractors, which can be performed by either internal or external auditors acting on the bank's behalf [S1]. These audits should assess the provider's performance, risk management practices, and regulatory compliance, with the frequency determined by the nature and extent of the risk [S3].
The selection of a group entity shall be based on objective reasons that are similar to the selection of a third-party [S1].
The bank or NBFC bears responsibility for the actions of its service provider, including Direct Sales Agents (DSAs) and recovery agents, as outsourcing does not diminish its obligations [S1][S2].

No, a commercial bank shall not engage a service provider outside its group if it is owned or controlled by any director, key managerial personnel, approver of the outsourcing arrangement, or their relatives [S1]. However, an exception to this requirement may be made with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight, and monitoring [S1].

According to [S1], sufficient compliance is achieved if there is clear separation and isolation of the bank's and its customer-specific data and information. This ensures that only personnel authorized by the bank can access the data belonging to them within a multi-tenant environment or architecture.

Yes, outsourcing arrangements entered into by a bank shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability to obtain redressal [S1]. Furthermore, the responsibility for redressal of customers’ grievances related to outsourced services shall rest with the bank [S3].

The outsourcing agreement must provide the bank with the right to conduct audits on the service provider, whether by its internal or external auditors or by agents appointed to act on its behalf, and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings made on the service provider in conjunction with the services performed for the bank [S2].

Yes, a commercial bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate, provided that the arrangement is backed by a Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs or agreements with its group entities are in place [S1].

Yes, your commercial bank may adopt a pooled (shared) audit with other regulated entities using the same third-party service provider, either by pooling audit resources or engaging an independent third-party auditor [S1]. However, it remains the responsibility of your bank to ensure that the audit requirements related to its specific contract with the service provider are met effectively [S1].

In addition to the general service provider evaluation criteria, banks must consider technology, infrastructural stability, data backup arrangements, disaster recovery plans, conflict of interest, and the capability to identify and segregate bank data [S1]. They must also assess the provider's ability to comply with regulatory and legal requirements, conduct information and cyber security risk assessments, and ensure appropriate controls for data protection and bank access [S1]. Furthermore, the evaluation should include the provider's ability to service all customers while maintaining confidentiality and enforce agreements regarding data storage, protection, and confidentiality [S1].

A commercial bank must create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains [S2]. Additionally, the bank is required to map its dependency on third parties and periodically evaluate the information received from these service providers [S2].

When establishing a viable contingency plan, a commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house during an emergency, along with the associated costs, time, and resources [S1].

The Board or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated is responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S1].

Yes, the provisions apply mutatis mutandis to subcontracted activities [S3]. Before granting consent, the bank must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with the Directions set out in Chapter III [S3].

Under the Reserve Bank of India's 2025 Directions, commercial banks are prohibited from outsourcing core management functions, which include Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions [S2]. These decision-making functions specifically involve determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and managing the investment portfolio [S2].

A bank must put in place a risk management framework that comprehensively deals with the processes and responsibilities for identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Additionally, the bank must have a management structure to monitor and control its outsourced services, including monitoring performance, uptime, service availability, adherence to SLA requirements, and incident response mechanisms [S3].

The Directions are titled "Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025" [S1]. The title explicitly indicates that Commercial Banks are the entities subject to these Directions [S1].

Commercial banks must ensure that their call centre staff are adequately trained to competently handle and escalate complaints as necessary [S1]. Additionally, the grievance redressal process must include a provision for the automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from the call center or base level to higher authorities [S1].
The co-branded card shall explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a co-branding arrangement [S1].

Card-issuers and their agents must adhere to the extant instructions on the Fair Practices Code for lenders [S2] and refrain from actions that could damage their integrity and reputation or violate strict customer confidentiality [S1].

No, prior approval of the Reserve Bank is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards, and co-branded credit cards, subject to the conditions stipulated under the relevant chapter [S1].

If no consent is received for activating the card, card-issuers shall close the credit card account without any cost to the customer within seven working days from the date of seeking confirmation from the customer [S2].
The monetary threshold is the lower of one percent of the credit limit or ₹5000 [S1].
The card-issuer must explicitly bring to the customer's notice that such information is being provided in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 [S1].
All communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number, and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact [S1].
A commercial bank may report a credit card account as 'past due' to credit information companies or levy late payment charges only when the account remains 'past due' for more than three days [S1].
No, commercial banks shall not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholders at the time of issue of the card and without getting their explicit consent [S1].

Yes, commercial banks may issue business credit cards to individuals for business expenses [S1]. These cards are specifically defined as being issued to business entities or individuals for the purpose of business expenses and not for personal use [S4].

Each card-issuer must have a well-documented policy approved by its Board or a delegated Committee that is available on its website and in consonance with RBI instructions [S1]. This policy should cover aspects such as interest rate ceilings, default reporting procedures, co-branding arrangements, blocking procedures, and grievance redressal frameworks [S9].

Card-issuers shall ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders [S1]. In case a cardholder protests any bill, the card-issuer must provide an explanation and, wherever applicable, documentary evidence within a maximum period of 30 days from the date of complaint [S1].

The card-issuer must provide the cardholder with a term-sheet containing the Master Information and Terms and Conditions (MITC), which details fees, charges, drawal limits, billing procedures, and default circumstances [S4]. Additionally, the issuer must provide the detailed procedure to report the loss, theft, or unauthorized use of the card or PIN [S69].

The disclosure of customers’ information to DSAs, DMAs, and recovery agents shall be limited to the extent that will enable them to discharge their duties [S1]. Personal information provided by the cardholder but not required for recovery purposes shall not be released by the card-issuer [S1].

A bank has the freedom to determine the interest on deposits accepted or renewed under the RFC Account Scheme, in accordance with a comprehensive policy on interest rates on deposits approved by its Board of Directors or a delegated committee [S1].
The bank must pay interest at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank, rather than at the contracted rate [S1].
The minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year, while the minimum tenor for NRO term deposits is seven days [S1].

A bank must have a comprehensive policy, duly approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated committee, that specifies the interest rates on deposits and penalties for premature withdrawals [S2]. Additionally, the bank must be authorized by the Reserve Bank of India under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) to accept such deposits [S1].

Yes, a commercial bank may, at its discretion, allow an additional interest of one per cent per annum over and above the scheduled rate on deposits held by its staff and their exclusive associations [S1].

A commercial bank must treat an NRE term deposit of a deceased depositor as a domestic rupee term deposit at maturity if the claimants of the account are residents [S1]. In such cases, interest for the subsequent period is paid at the rate applicable to a domestic term deposit of similar maturity [S1].

The rate of interest on matured deposits standing in the name of a deceased individual depositor shall be as per the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits and subject to the conditions laid down in paragraph 7 of the Directions [S2].

If the components of the penalty are not clearly brought to the notice of the depositors at the time of acceptance, the exchange loss arising out of premature withdrawal shall be borne by the bank [S1].

If the period from the date of maturity till the date of renewal does not exceed 14 days, the rate of interest payable shall be the appropriate rate for the renewal period as prevailing on the date of maturity or on the date when the depositor seeks renewal, whichever is lower [S1].
Yes, any action taken or purported to have been taken under the repealed Directions shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S1].

A bank is prohibited from charging a penalty for premature withdrawal of a domestic term deposit in the event of the depositor's death [S1], when splitting the amount at the request of claimants or joint holders without changing the period or aggregate amount [S2], or when depositors of a specific branch transfer their business to another bank [S5].

Yes, a bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staffs who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates admissible to senior citizens over and above the additional interest payable to them for being retired members of the bank’s staff [S1].
The minimum credit balance in a farmer's composite cash credit account is measured during the period from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month [S1].

A comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors must cover the interest rate on deposits and penalties for the premature withdrawal of term deposits, including partial withdrawals, as well as specific penalties for NRE and FCNR(B) term deposits [S4]. Additionally, the policy must ensure that the components of these penalties are clearly communicated to depositors at the time of acceptance [S1][S3].

Yes, a bank shall pay interest at the time of conversion of an FCNR(B) Account into an RFC or Resident Rupee Account even if the deposit has not completed the minimum maturity period [S1]. However, the rate of interest paid shall not exceed the rate payable on savings bank deposits held under the RFC Account Scheme [S1].

Banks are permitted to use foreign currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB and foreign currency funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market to grant PCFC [S3].

The bank must satisfy itself that the credit is against an export order, aligns with trade practices for the specific goods, and is an approved method of realising export proceeds [S1]. Additionally, the bank must ensure that the pre-shipment credit is liquidated out of the proceeds of bills drawn for the exported commodities [S4].

The exposure of a bank by way of PCEs to bonds issued by each such NBFC or HFC shall be restricted to one per cent of capital funds of the RE within the extant single or group borrower exposure limits [S1].

Under the RBI’s Commercial Banks – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025, all corporates and other constituent borrowers having a turnover above the threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors are mandated to disclose an aging schedule of their overdue payables [S1].

The bank must grant export credit to exporters of good track record until the realization of proceeds from the cheque or draft, provided the bank is satisfied that the instrument is against an export order, complies with trade practices for the goods, and is an approved method of realization under extant rules [S1].

The bank must take into account the customer's suitability and appropriateness for the product [S1]. Additionally, it must ensure that the borrowers or customers are made fully aware of the risks and liabilities associated with such products [S1].

The bank must verify the documents to the title of the property mortgaged with the bank regarding their genuineness at the time of their acceptance [S1]. Additionally, the bank should obtain market reports on builders or developers and ensure loans are sanctioned only for projects undertaken by reputed builders or developers [S1].

The builder, developer, or company must disclose the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged and indicate that they will provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC) or permission from the mortgagee bank for the sale of flats or property, if required [S1].

Yes, commercial banks shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies or other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing [S1]. This restriction is also reiterated in the conditions for departmental equipment leasing, which state that a bank shall not enter into leasing agreements with another equipment leasing company or other non-banking finance company engaged in equipment leasing [S2].

Bills rediscounted 'with recourse' in the domestic market should not be reckoned as export credit by the rediscounting bank, as only the first bank discounting the bills has recourse to the exporter [S1].

Gold or silver accepted as collateral shall be valued based on the reference price corresponding to its actual purity (caratage) [S2]. This reference price is the lower of the average closing price for that specific purity over the preceding 30 days or the closing price on the preceding day, as published by the India Bullion and Jewellers Association Ltd. (IBJA) or a SEBI-regulated commodity exchange [S2].

Under the RBI Directions, all collateral-free loans provided to low-income households with an annual income up to ₹3,00,000 are considered microfinance loans [S5]. To ensure the collateral-free nature of these loans, they must not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by the hypothecation of any security [S5].

Commercial banks must capture and maintain project-specific data in an electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis [S1]. This database must include, at a minimum, parameters for the debtor profile, the original project profile, and any changes in the Date of Commencement of Commercial Operations (DCCO) [S1].
No, a commercial bank is not allowed to grant finance for the construction of buildings meant purely for Government or Semi-Government offices, which explicitly includes Municipal offices [S1].

A commercial bank shall accept DLG only in one or more of the following forms: cash deposited with the bank, a fixed deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, or a bank guarantee in favour of the bank [S1].

An internet banking channel is defined as a digital banking channel offered over the internet, including web browser-based applications but excluding mobile applications [S1]. In contrast, a mobile banking channel is offered using mobile applications, unstructured supplementary service data (USSD), and short message service (SMS) [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may grant an extension of time to comply with or exempt any regulated entity from all or any of the provisions of the Directions, either generally or for a specified period [S1]. This exemption is subject to such conditions as the Reserve Bank may impose [S1].

Commercial banks must comply with the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements, including FEMA 1999 and applicable Reserve Bank instructions [S1]. The jurisdiction for legal settlement must be within India [S1].

Banks must obtain prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India and fulfill specific eligibility criteria, including implementing CBS with IPv6 support, meeting CRAR requirements, and demonstrating adequate financial and technical capabilities [S1]. The application for this approval must be submitted to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India, through the PRAVAAH portal [S1].

Yes, banks must obtain explicit consent from the customer for registering for digital banking services and clearly indicate that SMS or email alerts will be sent to the customer's registered mobile number or email for both financial and non-financial operations [S1].
Yes, you can rely on the RBI's interpretation, as the interpretation of any provision of these Directions given by the RBI shall be final and binding [S1].

Commercial banks offering digital banking services must comply with the Guidelines on Outsourcing of Information Technology Services specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Additionally, if a bank adopts an outsourced model for its digital banking operations, it must specifically adhere to the relevant regulatory guidelines on outsourcing contained in these same Directions [S2].

To be eligible to provide a view-only banking facility, the bank must have implemented a Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled its public-facing IT infrastructure to handle Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) traffic [S1].

Banks shall put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels that account for all statutory and regulatory requirements, including those related to the management of liquidity and operational risks in a digital banking scenario [S1].

Yes, banks must comply with various other regulatory guidelines, including those on IT outsourcing, IT governance, digital payment security, cyber security, and fraud risk management [S2]. Additionally, banks are required to adhere to the guidelines on customer protection and responsible business conduct as specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 [S3].

The passages do not specify which categories of banks are required to comply with the Directions, only stating that "All banks offering digital banking services" must comply with the general guidelines [S1].

The bank should consider lodging a formal complaint against the statutory auditors with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) or the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) [S1]. Additionally, pending disciplinary action, the complaints must be forwarded to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) after satisfying the bank of the auditors' involvement and providing them an opportunity to be heard [S1].
The responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank [S1].

The bar on additional credit facility to a wilful defaulter or any entity with which the wilful defaulter is associated shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of the wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters [S1].

The name of a borrower or guarantor classified as a wilful defaulter must be removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters after the implementation of the resolution plan under the IBC or the RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, provided the resolution results in a change in the management and control of the entity or business enterprise [S2].

A commercial bank shall put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identification of wilful defaulters so that the penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated [S1].

A commercial bank must submit information on wilful defaulters to all credit information companies at monthly intervals [S1]. The report must include a list of wilful defaulters for both suit filed accounts and non-suit filed accounts, as detailed in Annex II [S1].

Before transferring the defaulted loan, the bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective, and if wilful default is observed, it must complete the classification process and report it to credit information companies before the transfer [S1]. A two-stage committee is not compulsory, but the process must ensure a thorough examination of wilful default aspects [S1].

The bank shall forward the details of these third parties to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, regardless of the bank's membership status with the IBA [S1]. Before reporting to the IBA, the bank must satisfy itself of the third parties' involvement and provide them with an opportunity to be heard, following a suitably recorded due process [S1].

Yes, when a default happens in making payment or repayment by the principal debtor, a bank shall be able to proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank of India may issue necessary clarifications to remove difficulties in the application or interpretation of the Directions [S1]. The interpretation of any provision given by the Reserve Bank shall be final and binding [S1].

Yes, a commercial bank must report to credit information companies the details of guarantors who have failed to honour their commitments when invoked [S1]. These guarantors shall be reported as large defaulters or wilful defaulters, as the case may be [S1].

These Directions are applicable to commercial banks, which include all banking companies, corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 [S4]. However, Small Finance Banks (SFBs), Local Area Banks (LABs), Payments Banks (PBs), and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are explicitly excluded from this applicability [S4].
A commercial bank must require its internal auditors to specifically look into adherence to instructions for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter [S1].

A bank shall remove the name of a wilful defaulter from the List of Wilful Defaulters only when the borrower has fully paid the compromise amount [S2]. Until such full payment is made, the name shall not be removed even if the outstanding amount falls below the threshold of ₹25 lakh [S2].
Yes, the provisions of these Directions are in addition to, and not in derogation of, the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions currently in force [S5].

A "director" is defined as the director of a company classified as a large defaulter or wilful defaulter who was associated with the company at the time when the acts of omission or commission by the company or its directors led to the default [S1]. This definition applies to both commercial banks and non-banking financial companies [S2].
NOT FOUND
A commercial bank covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) must comply with the directions provided under that Scheme [S1].
The Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act (CICRA) provides the statutory backing for sharing credit information by a Credit Information (CI) with Credit Information Companies (CICs) [S1].
A commercial bank must undertake a half-yearly review of the Data Quality Index (DQI) for all segments [S1].

A commercial bank shall include suitable provisions in its loan policies and credit appraisal processes for obtaining Credit Information Reports (CIRs) from one or more Credit Information Companies (CICs) [S1]. This ensures that credit decisions are based on the credit information available in the system [S1].

Under the RBI Credit Information Reporting Directions, the term 'Company' is defined as a company defined under section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 or the corresponding section under the Companies Act, 2013 [S1].
For the commercial segment, a commercial bank must use Form 2, known as the Uniform Credit Reporting Format (Commercial) [S1].
The convenor must send the meeting agenda and notes at least fifteen (15) days before the scheduled meeting [S1].
The collection and reporting of credit information in respect of SHG members is restricted to the members of those SHGs that take loans exceeding ₹1,00,000/- [S1].
NOT FOUND
Meetings of the Technical Working Group (TWG) shall be held at least once in a calendar year [S1].

The Technical Working Group (TWG) comprises representatives from Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, All India Notified Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Housing Finance Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, India Banks’ Association, Micro Finance Institutions Network, Sa-Dhan, and CICs [S1].

If a term is not defined in the Directions, it shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in CICRA, 2005, the Credit Information Companies Rules, 2006, and the CIC Regulations [S5]. If the term is not defined in those sources either, it shall have the meaning assigned to it in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, or the Companies Act, 2013 [S5].
No, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks are not covered by these Directions, as the definition of 'Commercial Banks' explicitly excludes them [S2].

A commercial bank must have a dedicated nodal point or official of contact for Credit Information Companies (CICs) to handle customer grievances and furnish their details, including email ID and telephone/mobile number, to the CICs [S1]. Additionally, the bank is required to inform the CICs of any changes in these nodal points or officials within five calendar days of such a change [S1].

You should not arrange the sanction, as a Non-Executive Director (NED) shall not approach Branch Managers directly to sanction loans or other facilities to any constituent [S4]. Instead, the sanction of individual loan applications and determining credit worthiness are the responsibilities of technical experts, i.e., bank executives [S4].

A public sector bank's Nomination and Remuneration Committee must consist solely of Non-Executive Directors (NEDs) [S1]. The Government of India nominee director and the director nominated under specific statutory provisions are explicitly excluded from serving on the Committee [S1].
NOT FOUND
A bank must obtain regulatory approval for additional roles or responsibilities of the MD&CEO or CEO through the Pravaah Portal [S1].
No person shall continue as the MD&CEO / CEO or WTD of a PVB beyond the age of 70 years [S1].

A Public Sector Bank shall institutionalise discussions between its management and the Board on the quality of internal control systems [S1]. Additionally, the Board must specifically pay attention to creating and sustaining a culture of control [S1].
A unit showing signs of incipient sickness is eligible for a nominee director if its aggregate working capital limit from the entire banking system is ₹1 crore and above [S1].

A PSB’s Board shall fulfil four major roles: overseeing the risk profile of the PSB, monitoring the integrity of its business and control mechanisms, ensuring expert management, and maximising the interests of its stakeholders [S1].
Yes, a Public Sector Bank may entrust the Chief Vigilance Officer with portfolios such as Inspection and Audit, Accounts, Planning and Development, and Legal matters [S1].

A bank proposing to amend its Articles of Association must obtain prior regulatory approval under Section 35B of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, through the Pravaah Portal before circulating the draft amendments to its shareholders or convening a meeting [S1].
Yes, the contents of the Master Direction must be read along with other relevant governing statutes. [S1]
Any action taken or initiated under the repealed governance directions shall continue to be governed by the provisions of those repealed directions [S3].

A proposal for the appointment of a new MD&CEO must be submitted to the RBI at least four months before the expiry of the term of office of the present incumbent [S1].

Under the RBI’s 2025 Directions, a commercial bank must determine interest rates on foreign currency advances in accordance with a comprehensive policy on interest rates that has been duly approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated committee [S1]. This requirement is also applicable to export credit in foreign currency, which must follow the bank's Board-approved policy subject to the relevant guidelines in the Directions [S4].
No, the change in tenor premium shall not be borrower specific or loan class specific, meaning it must be uniform for all types of loans for a given residual tenor [S2].
Yes, the directions contained in paragraph 6 are applicable to Rupee advances granted against FCNR(B) deposits to a third party [S1].

Under the RBI's 2025 directions, an external benchmark rate includes the Reserve Bank of India policy Repo Rate, Government of India Three-months and Six-months Treasury Bill yields published by Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL), and any other benchmark market interest rate published by FBIL [S1].
The interest rate under an external benchmark shall be reset at least once in three months [S1].

The Board-approved policy must delineate the components of spread charged to a customer and include principles for determining the quantum of each component, the range of spread for a given borrower category or loan type, and the delegation of powers regarding loan pricing [S1].
Any action taken or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S3].
The MCLR prevailing on the date of the first disbursement, whether partial or full, applies to the loan until the next reset date [S1].
A commercial bank must review its Base Rate at least once in a quarter [S1].

A bank must have a comprehensive policy on interest rates on advances, including the pricing of microfinance loans, that is duly approved by the Board of Directors or a committee to which such powers have been delegated [S2]. Additionally, the bank must maintain a Board-approved policy that delineates the components of the spread charged to customers [S3].

A bank may calculate its cost of funds using the average cost of funds, marginal cost of funds, or any other reasonable and transparent methodology in vogue [S3]. The chosen method must be consistent and made available for supervisory review or scrutiny as required [S3].

Existing loans and credit limits linked to the Base Rate or BPLR shall continue till repayment or renewal, rather than automatically converting to MCLR [S1]. However, existing borrowers have the option to move to an MCLR-linked loan at mutually acceptable terms [S1].

Yes, a commercial bank may increase the credit risk premium charged to an existing borrower if the customer's credit risk profile has deteriorated [S1]. This is further supported by the provision that the spread charged to an existing borrower shall not be increased except on account of such deterioration [S2].

All floating rate rupee loans sanctioned and renewed on or after April 1, 2016, must be priced with reference to the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) [S1]. This rate serves as the internal benchmark for such purposes [S1].

Negative carry on the mandatory CRR is calculated using the formula: Required CRR x (marginal cost) / (1- CRR) [S1]. The marginal cost of funds used in this calculation is the one arrived at as per paragraph 17 [S1].

The Directions repeal existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines specifically relating to Interest Rates on Advances as applicable to Commercial Banks [S3]. However, the passages do not state that these Directions override or replace other existing laws and regulations that apply to commercial banks [S1].

No, the Customer Acceptance Policy shall not result in the denial of a financial facility to members of the general public, especially those who are financially or socially disadvantaged, including Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) [S1].

Yes, as an NBFC that is part of a group, you are required to implement group-wide programmes against money laundering and terror financing, including policies for sharing information for client due diligence and risk management [S1].
The NBFC shall put in place a system of periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts with a periodicity of at least once in every six months [S1].

An NBFC is not required to identify and verify the identity of any shareholder or beneficial owner if the customer or the owner of the controlling interest is an entity listed on a stock exchange in India, an entity resident in notified jurisdictions and listed on stock exchanges there, or a subsidiary of such listed entities [S1].

The Board of Directors of the NBFC, or any committee to which the Board has delegated power, must duly approve the KYC policy [S1]. This indicates that the Board can delegate this responsibility to a committee [S1].
If a non-profit organisation customer is not already registered, the NBFC shall register the details on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog [S1].

The NBFC shall carry out periodic 'Money Laundering (ML) and Terrorist Financing (TF) Risk Assessment' exercises to identify, assess, and mitigate risks, ensuring the process considers all relevant risk factors and sector-specific vulnerabilities [S1]. Additionally, the NBFC's policy framework must ensure compliance with the PML Act and Rules, providing a bulwark against threats arising from money laundering and terrorist financing [S2].

The NBFC must verify the UNSC Sanctions Lists and the lists in the Schedules to the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism (Implementation of Security Council Resolutions) Order, 2007, on a daily basis [S2]. This daily verification ensures that any modifications, such as additions or deletions, are taken into account for compliance [S2].

For opening an account of a partnership firm, the NBFC shall obtain certified copies of the registration certificate, partnership deed, PAN of the firm, documents relating to the beneficial owner or authorized persons, the names of all partners, and the address of the registered office and principal place of business [S1].

If an NBFC suspects money laundering or terrorist financing and reasonably believes that performing the CDD process will tip off the customer, it shall not pursue the CDD process and instead file an STR with FIU-IND [S1].

An individual customer is required to provide their Aadhaar number to an NBFC if they are desirous of receiving any benefit or subsidy under a scheme notified under section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016 [S2]. In all other cases, customers may provide the Aadhaar number voluntarily [S2].

An NBFC must obtain any two of the following documents as proof of business for a proprietary firm: registration certificates, municipal licenses, tax returns, GST/VAT certificates, professional body licenses, complete income tax returns, or utility bills [S1]. If furnishing two documents is not possible, the NBFC may accept only one document at its discretion, provided it undertakes contact point verification and confirms the business activity from the firm's address [S2].
An NBFC must verify the UNSCR 1718 Sanctions List of Designated Individuals and Entities every day [S1].

Under the RBI's KYC Directions, an NBFC is required to undertake ongoing due diligence of customers to ensure that their transactions are consistent with the NBFC's knowledge of the customers, their business, risk profile, and the source of funds or wealth [S1].
Yes, an NBFC has the option to hold 'pooled' accounts managed by professional intermediaries on behalf of entities like mutual funds or pension funds [S1].

No, the NBFC does not need to perform a fresh CDD exercise for identification in this case [S1]. The CDD procedure is applied at the Unique Customer Identification Customer (UCIC) level, so an existing KYC-compliant customer opening another account or availing a new product from the same NBFC is exempt from a fresh identification process [S1].

A loan is treated as commercial real estate exposure if it is made to builders, developers, or others for office buildings, retail space, hotels, land acquisition, or similar premises where repayment depends primarily on asset-generated cash flows [S2]. Additionally, loans for a third dwelling unit onwards to an individual are also classified as CRE exposure [S2].
The first mandatory performance review for a demand or call loan must occur within a cut-off date not exceeding six months from the date of sanction [S1].

EMI programmes on credit cards offered by an NBFC are governed specifically by the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, and such transactions are not covered under the Credit Facilities Directions [S1].
The cooling-off period for a digital loan must be determined by the NBFC in terms of their credit policy, subject to the period not being less than one day [S1].
The total amount of DLG cover on any outstanding portfolio specified upfront shall not exceed five per cent of the total amount disbursed out of that loan portfolio at any given time [S1].
For an NBFC, a microfinance loan is defined as a collateral-free loan given to a household having an annual household income up to ₹3,00,000 [S4].

An NBFC is required to make the prescribed disclosures in the 'Notes to Accounts' to the financial statements [S1]. This requirement is reiterated in the directions for credit facilities and resolution of stressed assets, which specify that disclosures must be made under 'Notes to Accounts' [S3][S5].
No, an NBFC shall not avail loans by re-pledging gold or silver pledged to it by its borrowers [S1].
No, an NBFC may enter into DLG arrangements only with an LSP or other lender engaged as an LSP [S1].
As an NBFC acting as a Default Loss Guarantee (DLG) provider, you must deduct the full amount of the DLG that is outstanding from your capital [S1][S2].

The NBFC must stipulate that the builder or developer discloses the name(s) of the entity to which the property is mortgaged in pamphlets, brochures, and on-site display boards, and appends this mortgage information in advertisements [S1]. Additionally, the builder or developer must indicate in their materials that they will provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC) or permission from the mortgagee entity for the sale of flats or property if required [S1].
Yes, Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) may publish the range of interest rates on microfinance loans charged by their members operating in a district as part of their awareness campaigns [S1].

An NBFC must announce the auction to the public by issuing advertisements in at least two newspapers, specifically one in a regional language and another in a national daily [S3]. Additionally, the NBFC must refrain from issuing misleading advertisements that contain unrealistic claims to promote loans against gold and/or silver collateral [S2].

The NBFC must have a due diligence process in place for the engagement of recovery agents, which includes verifying the antecedents of the individuals involved, such as police verification [S5]. Additionally, the NBFC must obtain an undertaking from the recovery agents to abide by the code of conduct [S4].

An NBFC shall store the collateral only in its branches that are manned by its employees and have safe deposit vaults fit for storing gold and silver [S1]. Such loans shall not be extended by branches that do not have appropriate secured facilities for the storage of the pledged eligible collateral [S1].

An NBFC must display on its website the methodology adopted for determining the net weight of the gold and silver content of the eligible collateral [S1]. It must also display the price used to value the gold and silver content for the determination of the LTV ratio [S1].

The borrowal accounts of other group companies, in which one or more promoter(s) or whole-time director(s) are common, must be subjected to examination by the concerned Regulated Entities from a fraud angle [S1].

In case of a suspicion or indication of wrongdoing or fraudulent activity, the Applicable NBFC shall use an external audit or an internal audit as per its Board approved Policy for further investigation in such accounts [S1].

An NBFC may withdraw an FMR or remove a perpetrator's name under exceptional circumstances, provided there is due justification and approval from an official at least in the rank of a director [S1]. Additionally, if the withdrawal is necessitated by Court directions, the NBFC may arrange for immediate withdrawal or removal and subsequently place the case before the official in the rank of WTD for information [S2].

The provided passages do not specify a minimum fraud amount for reporting incidents to law enforcement agencies; they only state that the Applicable NBFC shall immediately report incidents of fraud to appropriate Law Enforcement Agencies [S1].

In cases involving very senior executives of an Applicable NBFC, the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) shall initiate the examination of their accountability and place it before the Board [S1]. These executives are prohibited from participating in the Board, ACB, or SCBMF meetings where their accountability is being considered [S1]. Additionally, for public sector NBFCs, such cases must also be referred to the Advisory Board for Banking and Financial Frauds (ABBFF) [S1].

For standard assets on microfinance loans, an NBFC-MFI must maintain provisioning in accordance with the instructions contained in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025, for the respective layer of the scale-based regulatory framework [S3].
An NBFC-MFI must adhere to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 [S5].

An NBFC-P2P shall comply with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices dated November 07, 2023 [S1]. This framework requires establishing a robust IT Governance structure integrated with the overall corporate governance, driven by IT strategy and built upon principles of value delivery, risk management, resource management, and performance management [S4].
An NBFC-P2P must conduct an information system audit of its internal systems and processes at least once in two years [S1].
Yes, an NBFC-P2P is allowed to make use of the ‘Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience’, as amended from time to time [S1].

The leverage ratio for an NBFC-P2P is calculated as the total outside liabilities divided by the owned funds [S4]. Customers’ funds lent or borrowed using the platform are not reckoned as outside liabilities of the platform [S1].

An NBFC-P2P must comply with the provisions of paragraphs 6(1), 6(2), 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025 [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5]. Additionally, prior written permission from the Reserve Bank is required for any allotment of shares that results in an aggregate holding of 26 per cent or more of the paid-up capital, any change in shareholding granting the right to nominate a Director, or changes in directors and management [S3].
